metadata.title: Null mean curvature flow and outermost MOTS

extraction_notes.note: The proof of Lemma 10 cites Lemma~\ref{kappaexists} (itself) among the a-priori estimates, evidently a typo for Lemma 9 (boundaryforkappa); the self-reference edges are marked mention and an edge from Lemma 9 was added.
Theorem 1 calls $\partial\Omega$ 'outer trapped', while every result it rests on assumes outer untrapped; the \label{main} sits after \end{Theorem} but resolves to Theorem 1.

The introduction previews $(**)$, $(*_\varepsilon)$, $(*_{\hat\varepsilon})$ and the translating-graph property; per one-node-per-repeated-statement only the fuller Section 3 versions are nodes (the numbered intro display (3) is kept as an equation).

$(**)$ is stated as 'describes the evolution' (claim) but serves as the defining equation, typed definition; the C-minimizing sentence both imports a definition and asserts $N_k$ satisfies it, typed external definition.
The monotonicity formula is announced in a bold paragraph and derived in running text with no formal statement; the announcement is the claim and the derivation its prose proof.

Theorems 20, 37 and 39 are argued in running text before they are stated; the proof spans were chosen from the first sentence of the argument to the lead-in sentence, and the proof of Theorem 39 contains Lemma 38 and its proof.
Claims 1-4 in the proof of Lemma 36 are author labels (steps) and also numbered, later-cited inline claims, so each is both a labelled step and a nested Level-1 claim.

The unnumbered labelled displays supbnd and measdef get no own nodes (they stay in Lemma 7 and the measures definition); historical and comparative discussion in Sections 1, 4 and 8.1 is not extracted.

nodes.statement: We will call a function u as in (ii) of Theorem~ a weak solution of (**) and its level sets (Sigma_t=\u=t\)_tge 0 a weak solution of (*) (see Definition~). Theorem~ (ii) then states that there exists a weak solution of (*) with initial condition Sigma_0=partialOmega, (Sigma_t)_tge 0, that converges to a generalized MOTS that lies outside the outermost MOTS. Note also that the fact that the outermost MOTS has the form Sigma_infty=partialOmega_infty, where Omega_infty is an open set, is not an assumption---this is always the case with Omega_infty being the union of all weakly outer trapped sets in M, that is open sets with weakly outer trapped boundary (i.e. satisfying theta^+le 0), as is shown in .

\label{weakMOTS} Let $E\subset M$ be a finite perimeter set. We will say that the reduced boundary of $E$, $\partial^*E$,  is a generalized MOTS if the following hold 
 \begin{itemize}
 \item $\mu_E=\mathcal{H}^n\hbox{ {\vrule height .25cm}{\leaders\hrule\hskip.2cm}}\hskip5.0\mu\partial^*E$ carries a generalized mean curvature vector $\vec H$  and
 \item For $\mathcal{H}^n$-a.e. point on $\partial^*E$
 \[\vec H+ P\nu=0\,,\,\,\text{where }P=\nu^i\nu^jK_{ij}\]
 and $\nu$ is the measure theoretic outer pointing unit normal to $\partial^*E$.
  \end{itemize}
 (See  \cite[Definition 16.5 and \S14]{LSgmt} for precise definitions of $\partial^*E$, $\vec H$ and $\nu$).

nodes.statement: If partial^* E is a generalized MOTS, then by Allard's regularity theorem (see also ) we infer that, away from a set of H^n-measure zero, partial^*E is a C^1,alpha hypersurface for any alphain (0,1). This implies that locally (away from a set of H^n-measure zero) it is the graph of a function that satisfies equation weakly, and using standard PDE methods we obtain that partial^* E is smooth, and thus a MOTS in the classical sense, away from a set of H^n-measure zero. Furthermore, since the mean curvature is bounded on the reduced boundary, we also have that if partial^* E is a generalized MOTS then H^n(partial Esetminuspartial^*E)=0.

nodes.raw_latex:
Let $\psi:M\times [0,T)$, for $T>0$ be a positive solution of the backward heat equation on $M\times [0,T)$ \[\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}=-\Delta\psi.\]
We prove a monotonicity formula for the integral of the function
\[\phi:=(4\pi (T-t))^\frac12\psi.\]


We have that
\begin{equation*}\frac{d}{dt}\,d\mu_t=-\vec H(\vec H+\vec P) d\mu_t=-H(H+P) d\mu_t
\end{equation*}
and 
\[\frac{d\psi}{dt}=\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}+\nabla\psi\cdot (\vec H+\vec P)=-\Delta \psi+\nabla^\bot\psi\cdot (\vec H+\vec P),\]
where $\nabla^\bot= \nabla\psi\cdot \nu$, $\vec H=-H\nu$ and $\vec P=-P\nu$.

Since $\partial\Omega$ is strictly mean convex and outer untrapped with respect to the outward pointing unit normal (so that on $\partial \Omega$ $H+sP>0$ for $s\in[0,1]$) we can use the classical barrier construction of Serrin, as presented in   \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01}, to obtain the desired boundary gradient estimate. Since equation $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$ is expressed in terms of the geometry of $\mathrm{graph}\hat{u}$, in order to utilize the outer untrapped condition of the boundary $\partial\Omega$, we re-write it instead in terms of the geometry of the individual level sets of $\hat{u}$. To this end, we multiply $(*_{\hat{\varepsilon},\kappa,s})$ by $v^3=\sqrt{1+|\nabla\hat{u}|^2}^3$ to obtain
\begin{align*}

Q(\hat{u}):=&
(1+|\nabla\hat{u}|^2)\left(g^{ij}-\dfrac{\nabla^i\hat{u}\nabla^j\hat{u}}{|\nabla \hat{u}|^2+1}\right)\nabla_{ij}\hat{u}\\
&-s\sqrt{1+|\nabla\hat{u}|^2}^3\left(g^{ij}-\dfrac{\nabla^i\hat{u}\nabla^j\hat{u}}{|\nabla \hat{u}|^2+1}\right)K_{ij}\\
&+\frac{s}{\varepsilon}(1+|\nabla \hat{u}|^2)-\kappa\hat{u}\sqrt{1+|\nabla \hat{u}|^2}^3,
\end{align*}
and decompose it, as in  \cite[(14.43)]{GT01}, into the following coefficients 
\begin{align}\label{levelset}
Q\hat u&=(\Lambda a^{ij}_{\infty}+a^{ij}_0)\nabla_{ij}\hat{u}+|\nabla\hat{u}|\Lambda b_{\infty}+b_0=0,
\end{align} 
where 
\[a^{ij}_{\infty}(x,z,p)=a^{ij}_{\infty}\left(x,\frac{p}{|p|}\right)=\left(g^{ij}-\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2}\right),\,\,a^{ij}_0=\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2},\,\,\Lambda=1+|p|^2,\]
\[b_{\infty}(x,z,p)=b_{\infty}\left(x,z,\frac{p}{|p|}\right)=-sK_{ij}\left(g^{ij}-\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|^2}\right)-\kappa z\]
and
\[b_0=-\kappa z\frac{\Lambda}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}-sK_{ij}\left(g^{ij}\frac{\Lambda}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}+\frac{p^ip^j}{|p|}\frac{\Lambda^{1/2}}{\Lambda^{1/2}+|p|}\right)+\frac{s}{\varepsilon}\Lambda.\]
Then
\begin{equation*}a^{ij}_{\infty}\left(x,\frac{\nabla\hat{u}}{|\nabla\hat{u}|}\right)\frac{\nabla_{ij}\hat{u}}{|\nabla\hat{u}|}+b^{ij}_{\infty}\left(x,u,\frac{\nabla\hat{u}}{|\nabla\hat{u}|}\right)=-(H+sP)-\kappa \hat{u}, 
\end{equation*}
where here $H+P$ is the null mean curvature of the {\it level sets} of $\hat u$ with respect to the outward pointing unit normal. We see that $b_{\infty}$ is non-increasing in $z$, and also that the correction terms $a_0$ and $b_0$, that arise when considering the curvature of the level sets instead of the graph, are of the order required by the structure condition (14.50) (see also (14.59)) of  \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01}. That is, $a_0^{ij}=o(\Lambda)$ and $b_0=o(|p|\Lambda)$ as $|p|\to\infty$. Furthermore, since $\partial \Omega$ is outer untrapped, we see that the boundary curvature condition (14.51) of  \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01} is also satisfied since $H-b_{\infty}=H+sP> 0$ at all points on the boundary $\partial\Omega$.  \cite[Theorem 14.6]{GT01} can then be applied, which implies the existence of an upper barrier at any boundary point, and which  depends on the mean curvature of the boundary, $K$ and the supremum bound of of $\hat{u}$ (given in Lemma~\ref{supest}). This finishes the proof of the lemma.

nodes.statement: It is interesting to observe that the elliptic regularization problem (*_hatvarepsilon) provides a new way to locate MOTS in space-time initial data sets with a mean convex, outer-untrapped hypersurface. nodes.statement: The idea of the proof is to create an upper barrier for the functions u_varepsilon at the boundary partialOmega, by bending the (short time) smooth solution of (*) with initial data partial Omega. This construction is similar to that in with the extra complication that here we do not have a supremum estimate for the solutions u_varepsilon (a construction of a barrier using the smooth solution was also used in Lemma~). Let F(cdot,t):partialOmegatimes[0,T)to M be the unique solution to (*), with initial condition F(cdot, 0)=Id_partialOmegatopartialOmega and let Sigma_t=F(partialOmega, t) (see Remark~ for the existence of F). Since the null mean curvature of the hypersurfaces remains positive (see Remark~), we obtain that Sigma _t_1cap Sigma_t_2=emptyset for t_1ne t_2. For any tauin (0, T) we define \[ Omega_tau=bigcup_0<t<tauSigma_tsubset Omega, \] and let u:Omega_tauto R^+ be defined by u(p)=tLeftrightarrow pin Sigma_t. Then, we have that u is a smooth solution of (**) over overlineOmega_tau and furthermore there exists some constant C_0>1 such that frac1C_0le |nabla u|le C_0\,\,,\,\,|nabla^2 u|le C_0 in overline Omega_tau. We choose 0<tau<T such that tau<frac12 and bend the smooth solution u of (**) to construct a supersolution of (*_varepsilon) that is zero on partialOmega and goes to infinity on the inner boundary Sigma_tau of Omega_tau. To this end, we define psi:[0, tau)to R^+ to be the following smooth increasing function psi(t)=2t+frac1tau-t-frac1tau. Then psi(0)=0, lim_ttotaupsi(t)=+infty and furthermore we have psi'(t)=2+frac1(tau-t)^2\,\,, psi''(t)=frac2(tau-t)^3. We will show that the function \[v(x)=psi(u(x))\] is a super solution of (*_varepsilon) in Omega_tau for sufficiently small varepsilon. Since u_varepsilon solves (*_varepsilon) with u_varepsilon=0 on partial Omega, this would then imply that u_varepsilonleq v on barOmega_tau and \[ sup_partial Omega|nabla u_varepsilon|le sup_partial Omega|nabla v|le left(2+frac1tau^2right) C_0,\] which proves the lemma with C=(2+tau^-2)C_0. $ u_{\varepsilon_k}\to u$  in $C^0({\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega)$,
as in Definition~\ref{weak} (see also Theorem~\ref{weak existence}). We define the function $U:\Omega_1\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ by
\[U(x,z)=u(x).\]
Note that $U\in C^{0,1}(\Omega_1\times\mathbb{R})$ and $U_{\varepsilon_k}\to U$ in $C^0(({\Omega_1}\cup\partial\Omega)\times\mathbb{R})$, where the functions  $U_{\varepsilon_k}$ are as in Definition~\ref{Ue}. We,

\[\widetilde E_t=\{(x,z)\in \Omega_1\times\mathbb{R}: U(x,z)>t\}= E_t\times\mathbb{R}\,,\,\,E_t=\{x\in \Omega_1:u(x)>t\}\]
and
\[\widetilde\Sigma_t=\partial \widetilde E_t=\Sigma_t\times\mathbb{R}\,,\,\,\Sigma_t=\partial E_t.\]
Finally,  for notational simplicity, the sets $\widetilde E_t^{\varepsilon_k}$ and $\widetilde\Sigma_t^{\varepsilon_k}$, as defined in Definition~\ref{Ue}, will be denoted by $\widetilde E_t^k$ and $\widetilde\Sigma_t^k$ respectively. Moreover, the upward pointing unit normal to $\widetilde\Sigma _t^k$ and its mean curvature will be denoted by $\nu_k$ and $H_t^k$ respectively, so that equation \eqref{MCet} now reads
\begin{equation}\label{MCet2}
H_t^k=\mathrm{div}\nu_k=-P(u_{\varepsilon_k})+\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\nabla u_{\varepsilon_k}|^2+1}},
\end{equation}

\[\int_{W\cap (F\setminus \widetilde E_t)} \nu_k^i\nu_k^j-\nu^i\nu^jd\mathcal{H}^{n+2}\stackrel{k\to \infty}{\longrightarrow}0.\]
Since $P(\nu_k)- P(\nu)= (\nu_k^i\nu_k^j-\nu^i\nu^j) K_{ij}$, this implies that the last term also tends to zero.

Finally, one can easily see that the same minimization property holds for $E_t$ in $\Omega_1$ as follows (cf. \cite[Corollary 5.7]{S08}). Let $W\subset \Omega$ be a compact set and let $F$ be a finite perimeter set such that $E_t\subset F$ and $F\setminus E_t\subset W$. Given any $\ell>0$, let $\widetilde F=(F\times(-\ell,\ell))\cup \widetilde E_t$. Using the minimization property of  $\widetilde E_t$, we have
\[|\partial^*\widetilde E_t\cap \widetilde W|+\int_{\widetilde W\cap \widetilde E_t} P(\nu)d\mathcal{H}^{n+2}\le |\partial^*\widetilde F\cap \widetilde W|+\int_{\widetilde W\cap \widetilde F} P(\nu)d\mathcal{H}^{n+2},\]
where $\widetilde W=W\times[-2\ell, 2\ell]$. This then yields
\[\begin{split}
2\ell|\partial^* E_t\cap W|+2\ell \int_{ W\cap  E_t} P(\nu)d\mathcal{H}^{n+1}\le& 2\ell|\partial^* F\cap  W|+2\mathcal{H}^{n+1}(F\setminus E_t)\\
&+2\ell \int_{W\cap  F} P(\nu)d\mathcal{H}^{n+1}.
\end{split}\]
Dividing by $\ell$ and letting $\ell\to \infty$ provides the required property.
